answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Many companies, including Google, are assessing opportunities to invest in clean energy in markets where they do not have operational electricity consumption, but where such investments can advance decarbonization. This is why we strongly support the development of credible methodologies to estimate the consequential emissions of actions that fall outside of company inventories, and to allow companies to be recognized for these interventions.

Consequential accounting fundamentally estimates the impact of an action relative to a counterfactual in which that action did not occur. As such, it is important that care is taken to develop estimation methodologies that can support credible claims and narrow the range of uncertainties that are inherent to counterfactual analysis.

We believe two areas of focus warrant prioritization for further development and refinement by the Actions & Market Instruments (AMI) Technical Working Group (TWG):

1. the appropriate emissions rates and calculation methodologies to be used for counterfactual analysis, and;
2. the importance of additionality in supporting credible claims to emissions impact.

We provide more detail on these two areas of focus in our responses to Questions 42 and 30, respectively.

Strong and credible guidance on emissions rates, calculation methodologies, and additionality are needed to improve upon the marginal emissions data that exists today, and to support feasibility and comparability. GHGP could also clarify the claims that can be associated with both attributional and consequential accounting methods to ensure that consumers of this information understand their differences. We encourage GHGP to collaborate closely with SBTi, ISO, and others on this topic to ensure the continued relevance of both attributional and consequential claims.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text: As the consultation document notes, secondary effects may be small in some cases, but could also be large enough to be relevant depending on the technology or location in question. We thus support the consideration of certain secondary effects in any consequential analysis of electricity sector projects.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: Robust, feasible additionality criteria are critical for credible impact accounting. This is because under impact accounting, companies will claim to have avoided emissions that would have otherwise occurred had they not taken an action (in this case, to purchase clean electricity). The AMI TWG will need to carefully develop additionality criteria that strike a balance between sufficient, verifiable rigor and pragmatism. In a recent public paper, Google has shared how we consider additionality within our own clean energy portfolio (see page 25) including through the use of long-term contracts and the provision of strategic capital for advanced technologies: https://www.gstatic.com/gumdrop/sustainability/accelerating-advanced-clean-electricity-technologies.pdf. However, this is not definitive; additionality is a nuanced topic requiring dedicated discussion with project developers, financiers, and offtakers to align criteria that will be sufficiently rigorous yet feasible for companies to share as part of a voluntary, public accounting framework.

answers.label: Other appropriate emission rates or metrics
answers.text:
There is a substantial body of literature identifying limitations in the use of short-run marginal emissions rates (SRMER). SRMER is an operational metric, intended to measure what is known as the “operating margin,” which is the change in a variable that an intervention would cause assuming that the electricity grid is fixed, without considering how an electricity system intervention (on either the load or generation side) impacts the longer-term structural evolution of the grid system. According to a paper by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589004222001857), this “can be a crucial omission if [SRMER] are being used to comprehensively characterize the consequences of an intervention—especially a long-lived intervention such as a home retrofit, vehicular electrification, energy efficiency measures, or proposed renewable generators.” As a result of not considering long-run effects, NREL finds that SRMER significantly overpredicts the emissions associated with an intervention (e.g. emissions are predicted to be higher than in reality).

We thus believe that credible consequential estimation methods should also incorporate long-run effects (the “build margin”) into the emissions rates used for counterfactual analysis and support further development of this dual approach within the AMI TWG, especially the appropriate weighting between short- and long-run factors. This will be critical to ensuring that consequential emissions estimates are both rigorous and reflective of real-world grid dynamics.

Beyond emissions rates, additional consequential methodology elements may warrant further examination. For example, we support the AMI TWG evaluating questions such as whether an induced emissions metric is necessary as part of the consequential framework.

answers.label: Why that temporal granularity ceiling
answers.text: Marginal emission rates are most accurate at the hourly or sub-hourly level.
